new_statements.quote: In contrast, the Mezquital Otomi phonological word is the domain in which interacting systems of stress and tone operate. The structure of the word nucleus (simple or complex) determines the rules by which basic tone sequences are modified. A balance of the following components (in ranked order) is crucial to word structure: stress, tone, length, nasalization, glottalization, and syllable release (controlled or ballistic).

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record has an empty rule; the abstract establishes that the language has word stress alongside tone (stress is the top-ranked component of the word), but gives no placement. The listed open_url (WALS refdb record 880) now resolves to Wang 1985 (Miaoyu jianzhi) - wrong item; the DOI resolves to Cambridge Core where only the abstract is open. new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract says Mezquital Otomi has both a stress system and a tone system operating within the phonological word, with stress ranked first among the word-structure components; the placement of stress is not stated in the abstract, and the full article could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Voigtlander and Echegoyen 1979 describes Otomi de la Sierra (Eastern Highland Otomi, ISO otm), a different variety from Mezquital Hñähñu. Neve y Molina 1767 is a colonial description whose place names cluster in southwestern Hidalgo and northern Mexico state; Boot (intro p. 8) argues from the self-designation 'Na nhiânhiû' that it records the Valle de Mezquital variety, but flags this as unconfirmed.

new_statements.quote: 17. Todos los vocablos de este Idioma, sean nombres, verbos, ù otra parte de oracion, se pronuncian largos en las ultimas sylabas, segun denota el acento, y los que no le tuvieren se pronuncian breves en dichas sylabas, y en esto se diferencia na yophnì largo, que significa la ahuja, de na yŏphni breve, que significa el Arriero, y assi otros muchos que dará à conocer la practica. [...] Observando tambien con toda diligencia las quantidades de cada sylaba, las que se demonstrarán por los acentos.
new_statements.translation: 17. All the words of this language, whether nouns, verbs, or other parts of speech, are pronounced long in their final syllables, as the accent indicates, and those that do not have it are pronounced short in those syllables; and in this 'na yophnì' long, meaning 'needle', differs from 'na yŏphni' short, meaning 'muleteer', and so many others that practice will make known. [...] Also observing with all diligence the quantities of each syllable, which will be shown by the accents.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened 107 pp). Extracted the embedded page images for PDF pages 31 and 32 with pdfimages (the box is at load 300 so page render stalled) and read them. PDF p. 31 = Reglas de Orthographia pp. 8-9, PDF p. 32 = pp. 10-11. Rule 17 on p. 8 reads exactly as quoted (long s printed as f-like glyphs, normalized to s as the reader states): 'Todos los vocablos de este Idioma, sean nombres, verbos, u otra parte de oracion, se pronuncian largos en las ultimas sylabas, segun denota el acento, y los que no le tuvieren se pronuncian breves en dichas sylabas, y en esto se diferencia na yophni largo, que significa la ahuja, de na yophni breve, que significa el Arriero, y as-' with the tail 'si otros muchos…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty, so nothing to agree with or contradict; the 1767 statement adds a pre-modern observation of a contrastive final-syllable 'long accent' (quantity/tone) in what Boot argues is the Mezquital variety. It should not be entered as a modern stress placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: An 18th-century missionary description: the 'accent' is a written mark of vowel quantity, and words are said to carry it (a 'long' pronunciation) on the final syllable, with unmarked words 'short' there; presence versus absence of the mark is lexically contrastive (needle vs muleteer). This is a statement about a final-syllable length/pitch contrast (what modern work treats as tone and length), not a statement of stress placement in the modern sense, so it cannot be mapped cleanly onto a stress reading; if read as prominence it points to the final syllable. Boot's own introduction (the only part with a text layer) says nothing about stress. No 'acento' mention was found by scanned anywhere in the Arte (pp. 97-160) or the front matter.
new_statements.exceptions: words without the accent mark are 'short' in the final syllable; the contrast is lexical (na yophnì 'needle' vs na yŏphni 'muleteer')
new_statements.identity_note: Voigtlander and Echegoyen 1979 describes Otomi de la Sierra (Eastern Highland Otomi, ISO otm), a different variety from Mezquital Hñähñu. Neve y Molina 1767 is a colonial description whose place names cluster in southwestern Hidalgo and northern Mexico state; Boot (intro p. 8) argues from the self-designation 'Na nhiânhiû' that it records the Valle de Mezquital variety, but flags this as unconfirmed.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction between opened sources, but they speak past each other: the Wallis 1968 abstract (modern, Mezquital) states that stress and tone are interacting systems within the phonological word without giving the placement, while Neve y Molina 1767 (via Boot 2005) describes a lexically contrastive 'long accent' on final syllables, which is a quantity/tone mark rather than stress. The one modern grammar in the list (Voigtlander and Echegoyen 1979) could not be downloaded and in any case describes Sierra (Eastern Highland) Otomi, not Mezquital. The placement of word stress in Mezquital Otomi was not recovered from the open copies.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.deciding_source_year: 2010 (grammar notes first published in the 2004 1st ed.)
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held ILV 2010 dictionary text at the stated locators (Bartholomew sec. 14, 14.1, 14.2 on pp. 514-515; introduction 'Tonos musicales' pp. xix-xx). (2) The classification rests on a 2010 SIL dictionary's grammar notes (Bartholomew) for exactly this variety: modern and specialist-authored but prosodically brief (two paragraphs), i.e. a dictionary-with-sketch, not a phonology. The dedicated Mezquital Otomi prosody literature (Sinclair & Pike 1948; Leon & Swadesh 1949; Wallis 1968; Bernard 1973/1974) is older, paywalled, not yet obtained, and analytically split (tone-only vs. accent vs. lexical stress+tone), as documented in the held Turnbull 2017 JIPA review
